Much of the specialization evidence is partly built into the method: experts are explicitly pretrained from GPT-4o domain labels, after which domain-aligned routing and sensitivity to removing a frequently used expert are expected. The ToM localizer fails to recover the Social expert, and the text claims to include general-expert localizer results that do not appear in Figure 5.

The controllability claim is not convincingly evaluated. Likewise, benchmark-specific removal of an expert selected as irrelevant by intuition is an oracle intervention rather than a generally usable steering procedure.

The neuroscience framing is substantially stronger than the evidence. The four coarse, overlapping categories are author- and GPT-defined mappings rather than demonstrated analogues of brain networks; no neural or behavioral alignment benchmark is used, and only two of three localizers behave as predicted. The contribution is consequently closer to supervised domain-specialized MoE training than a validated brain-like architecture.

Key architectural details are too ambiguous for technical verification or reproduction. It is unclear whether all experts compute attention keys/values while only the routed expert computes the feed-forward block, how autoregressive caches are maintained, how top-1 routing receives gradients, and how ablation or top-k mixing is implemented. Parameter counts, active parameters, FLOPs, memory, router dimensions, load balancing, sequence lengths, decoding settings, checkpoint selection, and released code/models are also missing.

Data and reporting inconsistencies raise additional validity concerns. The main text says 1,000 examples were sampled from each of 19 datasets, whereas the appendix reports only 3,055 total examples with much smaller per-source counts. Stage-1 data include GSM8K, MATH, and closely related social-reasoning datasets, but training splits and decontamination against evaluation sets are not documented. EMPATHY is named as an evaluation benchmark but receives only routing analysis.

The test-time scaling claim is not robust across backbones: top-2 routing improves OLMo but reduces Llama's reported average from 36.3 to 35.4. Several statistical practices are under-specified or questionable. Reasoning results appear to come from one training run, with standard errors over benchmark items rather than training variability. CogBench uses a changed evaluation protocol and a new aggregate score without statistical comparisons; its claimed bound also fails for negative normalized scores.

Expert deletion is confounded by routing frequency and removal of computation: if math tokens are routed to the logic block, deleting that block will naturally hurt math, but this does not by itself demonstrate that its representations acquired a uniquely logical function. There is no neural-data evaluation, while the MD-to-logic and DMN-to-world-knowledge mappings are substantial simplifications.

The localizer evidence is mixed: the language localizer favors the world expert in later layers, and the ToM localizer does not reliably recover the social expert. No comparison shows that MICRO aligns better than an ordinary domain-specialized modular model.

Crucial controls are missing, including shuffled expert labels, arbitrary or conventional domain partitions, matched stage-wise training without neuroscience labels, alternative expert counts, and stage-by-stage ablations. Consequently, the experiments do not isolate any benefit specific to the proposed cognitive organization.

The performance claims are overstated. In Table 3, the dense baseline beats unablated MICRO on seven of eight benchmarks for both Llama-3.2-1B and Llama-3.2-3B. Figure 7 partly relies on selecting the best expert ablation per MMLU/BBH subtask, without a held-out selection rule, effectively creating an oracle comparison.

The statistical evidence is inadequate: reasoning results appear to come from single trained checkpoints; benchmark-item standard errors do not capture training variance; Welch tests do not account for paired predictions or the many comparisons; and several auxiliary tables provide no uncertainty.

Expert ablations do not by themselves demonstrate causal semantic specialization: removing the expert receiving most tokens necessarily removes task-relevant capacity. Traffic-matched, random-expert, rerouting, and parameter-matched controls are needed.

The claimed fine-grained steering is supported by only four cherry-picked examples and no quantitative measure of control, correctness, or quality degradation. Figure 23 contains an unrelated World-expert response about a late friend for a pizza-allocation prompt, indicating a serious quality-control problem.

Human-alignment evidence is fragile. The paper changes CogBench inference, introduces a new aggregate score without sensitivity analysis, reports scale-dependent gains that disappear for smaller models, and gives no significance test. Routing correlations lack confidence intervals, multiple-testing correction, or baseline comparisons, and the logic expert cannot be evaluated with the chosen annotations.

Cloning every transformer block into four experts roughly quadruples block parameters and storage. Reporting only active parameters obscures this cost; no memory, latency, throughput, or equal-total-parameter dense comparison is provided.

Reproducibility is limited by absent code/checkpoints, hardware and compute reporting, incomplete router and ablation details, undocumented split/decontamination procedures, and reliance on proprietary O1, GPT-4o, and GPT-5 outputs. Overall, the work is a promising domain-specialized modular prototype, but its neuroscience interpretation, performance narrative, and controllability claims are not sufficiently supported for acceptance.

strengths: The three-stage curriculum is simple and potentially useful: only 3,055 curated examples seed specialization that largely persists through full-scale instruction tuning.

The study covers several model families and scales and includes dense and architecture-matched modular controls, standard reasoning benchmarks, CogBench, routing analyses, localizers, and expert ablations.

The strongest results provide credible evidence of semantic modularity: language and logic routing is clear in the larger models, and ablating those experts causes domain-consistent performance losses.
The appendix usefully reports data composition, prompts, standard-MoE failure cases, and preliminary DPO and domain-specific tuning experiments.
weaknesses: The central “brain-like” interpretation is not established. The four domains are manually chosen analogies rather than validated computational counterparts of brain networks, no neural data are used, the language localizer shifts toward the world expert, and ToM localization is weak. The main synthetic routing probes are especially circular: GPT-5 is instructed using the same network descriptions used to produce the training labels and explicitly asked to generate examples activating only one expert.

Essential controls are missing: stage-by-stage curriculum ablations, shuffled or arbitrary expert labels, alternative semantic partitions, routing-load-matched ablations, and comparisons with existing specialization methods. Removing a heavily routed expert also removes substantial computation, so the resulting drop does not by itself demonstrate unique functional specialization. No domain-specific performance ablation convincingly establishes causal roles for the social and world experts.

The performance claim is overstated. In Table 3, full MICRO trails Dense on 21 of 32 entries and has a lower eight-task mean for three of four reported backbone groups. Some headline gains require post-hoc expert removal; for MMLU and BBH, the best expert is selected separately on test subtasks, yielding an optimistic oracle result rather than a deployable comparison.

Evidence for human alignment is inconsistent. The paper introduces an unvalidated aggregate metric, reports no significance analysis for its apparent gains, omits OLMo from CogBench, and shows Dense outperforming MICRO on both smaller SmolLM2 models. Human-rating correlations lack uncertainty and multiple-testing analysis, use hand-selected expected correspondences, and are weak for several claimed experts.

Controllability is supported only by a few selected qualitative examples without human or task-based evaluation. Some interventions visibly damage quality; notably, the world-only response to the pizza prompt repeats an unrelated answer about being late to a meeting.

The statistical analysis is inadequate: model-training variance is not measured, Welch tests ignore the paired nature of predictions on identical examples, many comparisons are uncorrected, and nonsignificance is treated as evidence of matching performance.

The practical and reproducibility story is incomplete. Full-block replication roughly quadruples stored backbone parameters, yet parameter counts, memory, attention/KV-cache costs, FLOPs, and throughput are absent. Router and ablation mechanics are underspecified, and no code, checkpoints, training seeds, hardware details, or complete proprietary-LLM generation settings are provided. The more economical standard-MoE variant fails to specialize at larger tested scales.
